speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that we have no representatives from our socialist Party in the House as we commence debate on this very important Bill this morning. I say that because while the Liberal Party must carry the main burden for the deficit financing that we are now into and the necessary borrowing which follows from such deficit financing, I think all Members of the House would agree that it is certainly the socialist Party that has egged the Government on month after month, year after year, into more and more irresponsible spending with the resulting deficits and borrowing requirements with which we are now faced.
One of the saddest things happening to us is that people are losing their perspective. They no longer can relate to $ 1 million, let alone to SI billion or to $30 billion of deficit financing or requirements. The perspective is so confused or fudged at the present time that the Government sees nothing wrong with coming before us, as it did in its last presentation in the form of a budget, and indicating that between the 1983-84 fiscal year and 1986-87 the total financial requirements of the nation will be $93 billion.
Let me repeat that figure: $93 billion is what the Government has put before us as its financial requirements in the sense of what it will have to borrow either during this fiscal year or through to fiscal year 1986-87. I mention that because is it not strange that we have a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), to whom many refer aptly as the emperor, who went to Williamsburg and had the colossal nerve to say to the United States of America, the United Kingdom, Germany, Japan and various other participants in the conference, "You had better get your deficit in line; you had better cut back on your spending"?
That was the representation on the part of our Prime Minister who only weeks ago, through his Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), told us that our own deficit requirement for financial needs between now and 1987 would be $93 billion. That on a per capita and gross national product basis is much higher than they have or are anticipated to have in the United States. For example, in Canada our deficit for fiscal 1983-84 will be $31.3 billion, more than we spent at the federal Government level in total in the fiscal year 1975. It is about triple, in deficit terms alone, the total spending when the emperor took power in this country in 1967-68.
I mention this little bit of background because our socialist friends to the left, who have been so instrumental in putting the spending in place, have not only been allowing the Government but egging it on to increase this deficit. I still hear the odd socialist say that it is right to spend, that the Government should be borrowing, that somehow or other deficit financing is the way of the future. That is not true.
There is all kinds of evidence that the dilemma we face in this country with high spending, low revenues and big deficits is actually deterring rather than encouraging growth in this country. Some may claim it is Keynesian to argue that the state should be spending, fine tuning-as they call it-the economy with such spending and deficit financing. I invite those who attribute that approach to Keynes to read what Keynes said with respect to such deficit financing as we are now experiencing. He would have been shocked that socialists of the day, such as those who sit to our left or the dear socialists opposite who presently form the Government, would attribute their irresponsibility with respect to deficit financing to something that they learned from Keynesian teaching.
What Keynes suggested was that in times of a slowdown, the state can spend and go into a deficit position in anticipation of going into a surplus position in better times. You then pay off whatever you incurred in the form of debt during the slow time and somehow you have a levelling. Perhaps where this Government went wrong is that it only heard one side of the equation.
In the early seventies, at the behest of the New Democratic Party, the Government put in massive spending programs. When we were in power, we learned that they did not even have the foresight to ask about the projected ongoing trends with regard to the cash requirements for those programs year after year.

I would like to return to my central theme, Mr. Speaker, but it is clear how the rabbles start to get roused here. The socialists are the most intolerant group in the House. They never like to hear the candid truth about the thrust of their policies discussed in public.
I believe that before any borrowing Bill is passed, we in Canada must insist that the Government present a more meaningful program for the reduction of the ongoing deficit that it foresees for the country. There is absolutely no reason why we should be placing an invisible mortgage on the future generations of the country, a mortgage amounting to some $93 billion of federal financial requirements between now and 1987.
If I had an opportunity to speak longer, Mr. Speaker, 1 would tell you about the effect that, if in power, we in this Party could have on the deficit by stressing the greater productivity in industry and by seeing that agricultural produce is exported to a greater extent. In short, if we could do these simple things, we could reduce unemployment, reduce the deficit, reduce inflation in the country and we could raise the real growth to over 5 per cent on average per year. In truth, we would bring back to Canada a realistic prosperity, a Conservative type of prosperity that would be built on responsible fiscal financing with less deficit financing than this socialist-Liberal conspiracy has been frustrating the nation with for too long.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it always amazes me that when a moderate like my colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), gives the House the benefit of his experience and his knowledge with respect to moderation in government spending, it causes shouting and disorder in the House on the part of the socialists to his left and the socialists across from him on the Government side. They have gone absolutely berserk and wild in response to this man who speaks only common sense.
As a Member of Parliament who attempts to represent a constituency from western Canada, I would like to carry on in the enlightened way of my colleague and try to bring to the House some semblance of perspective with respect to the Government's spending program. For a number of very legitimate reasons, this spending program is causing very serious and deeply felt concern for the people I represent.
The Hon. Member for York-Peel has made reference to the meeting of the leaders of the industrialized seven in Williamsburg, Virginia. He has pointed out quite rightly that there was a rather unusual and almost unbelievable intervention on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the course of those discussions. During the course of the discussions, as reported widely by the press, the Prime Minister joined with other leaders in railing against the extent of the deficit in the United States. One must ask oneself who is fooling whom.
This is the seventh time in this session that the Government has brought a borrowing Bill before the House to ask for additional funds over and above those it planned to spend in terms of an increasingly enlarged deficit. On each occasion that the Government comes before the House to seek borrowing authority, we find ourselves in a more deteriorated economic circumstance. The Government cries to the Opposition that it is in dire straits and in dire need of additional funds. This having happened on seven occasions, the only conclusion one can come to is that the Government is incapable of dealing with the economy of the country. That seems to be a selfevident fact. Why are we becoming more and more reliant upon borrowing Bills to carry on the day-to-day activities of the Government?
I was interested in the final communique issued from Williamsburg because it referred to the debt situation. After deliberation, the seven leaders stated that they viewed with concern the international financial situation and especially the debt burdens of many developing nations. The concern that should have been expressed is for the debt burden being experienced not by the developing antions but by the western industrialized nations. That is a matter of great concern to many Canadians.
In western Canada where I come from deficit financing and the great debt are viewed with alarm and skepticism. The Prime Minister increased spending from $12.6 billion in 1968 to approximately $100 billion in 1983-84. Our deficit will be in excess of $25 billion for at least each of the next four years. Yet the Government is back for the seventh time asking permission to borrow money. Its obligations amount to $26.7 billion but it already has $16 billion in borrowing authority. Now it is asking to borrow $4 billion more than the $10.7 billion it needs to meet requirements.
One has to ask why the Government is asking for these additional funds when, clearly, they are not needed at this time. As a humble country boy from western Canada, I can only conclude that there is the prospect of an election sooner or later. The Government wants to get into a position where it can have a slush fund available if an election comes within the next few months. I ask Hon. Members opposite why the Government is asking for $4 billion more than it requires. There is only one answer, Mr. Speaker: it needs the money to try to buy its way back into power in a future election.
That $4 billion is an interesting figure, Mr. Speaker. In western Canada people realize that is the amount of the

The people of western Canada, the livestock producer, the grain producer, are looking at this Government in terms of the way in which it manages or mismanages its affairs, and because they are very wise people out there, they say to themselves: "We are not prepared to change what we now have for something which we describe out here as a 'pig in a poke'."
We have seen the way this outfit operates, the way it reneges on its commitments. It promised $4 billion to be expended to increase the industrial and manufacturing base in western Canada, yet not a cent has been committed under this program, of which I am aware, in any tangible way towards that objective. Where is the basis upon which we can expect anything from this Government that is not almost a matter of being enshrined in the Constitution, Mr. Speaker? I am looking forward to the amendments to the legislation which the Minister of Transport has promised for us today to see what exactly he has in mind. I see, Mr. Speaker, I have only a short period of time left. I look forward to the opportunity to carry on this debate. The Government seems to have quite a double standard, Mr. Speaker. If you go to a bank or to Household Finance to borrow money, one of the requirements that both this Government and the provincial Governments have laid on the lender is that before the borrower signs on the dotted line he has to be told exactly what the loan is going to cost him. Now, would it not be a unique experience if this Government were required to tell all the taxpayers of Canada exactly what its borrowing is going to cost them? Would it not be unique if each of the taxpayers could say to this Government: "We will not lend you this money until you explain to us how much this is going to cost us"?
The cost to the taxpayer, Mr. Speaker, is going to be astronomical. As the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has already pointed out, this year alone we have gone in hock for $31 billion, much of which is probably not necessary at this point. At that rate of borrowing the national debt is going to double over four years. We are already paying 25 cents out of every tax dollar just to pay the interest on the national debt. Imagine what that is going to do to the poor taxpayer out there given the borrowing trend we face in this country. It would be in the interests of fairness and equity to the taxpayer if he was able to extract from the Government some kind of statement about exactly what this is going to cost him.
As I have said a number of times in the House, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to repay this debt. There is not a Member in this House who is going to help repay this debt. Neither will our children. It is our grandchildren who will begin paying off this debt. That is the interest; I wonder if they will ever get a chance to start paying the principle.
If you borrow money in the business world you have to have some assets against which the borrowing takes place. But this Government's borrowing is like borrowing against the groceries. It is like some of the fishermen in my riding who would borrow money to pay for gasoline or groceries when they go on a fishing trip. They burn up the fuel, eat the groceries and afterwards there is nothing which the lender can attach to cover the debt. They cannot attach the boat or the fish or anything. The Government has spent this money and there is nothing which can be attached. It seems to me that we are in deep trouble, Mr. Speaker.
My friends to the left, who are always so interested in borrowing, should realize that there is a fundamental tenet in the borrowing world-that when you start putting yourself into debt you become at least a partial prisoner of your creditor. My friends to the left are always harping on the need for Canada to express its economic independence. Since this is the fourth time this fiscal year that the Government has come to us for borrowing authority, we need to ask ourselves how much is owned to Canadian citizens and institutions and then now much is owed by the Government to foreign institutions. I wonder if the financial critic for the NDP, the Hon. Member
for Kamloops-Shuswap, has any idea of how much we owe to Wall Street bankers.

Once again, 1 welcome this opportunity to participate in a debate on the Government's borrowing authority. This particular Bill, which would authorize the Government to borrow another $14.7 billion, comes hot on the heels of the last appeal to Parliament for borrowing authority. A little more than three months ago, the Government asked for authority to borrow $19 billion. At that time Members of Parliament were asked to authorize that gang over there to borrow $14 billion for this fiscal year without even knowing what the money would be spent on. Therefore, when the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) proclaimed as he introduced the Bill that this time Hon. Members would be told where the money would be spent, 1 found his self-righteousness a little hard to understand. Of course the Government told us this time what the money would be spent on. However, it should do that each time it requests authority to borrow money. The Minister really has no right to puff up his chest as if the Government had done Parliament some great favour by telling us how it will spend the money.
When we add it up-the $14.7 billion the Government wants to borrow under the Bill, the $14 billion borrowed for this fiscal year under the last Bill, as well as the $2 billion left over in borrowing authority from last year-we find that the Government is asking to borrow over $30 billion, a tidy little sum. 1 would not begrudge this to the Government if I were convinced that it would be invested wisely in economic recovery, if it were invested in putting Canadians back to work and, by so doing, increasing the Government's tax revenues, reducing its expenditures on Unemployment Insurance and welfare. However, I am not convinced of that.
Borrowing Authority
In spite of the grandstand statements about recovery and job creation in the April budget, all that is evident is that the Government plans to wait the recession out, hoping that it can claim credit for recovery when the recession is over. However, when the business cycle begins its upturn, the Government will surely not be able to claim any of the credit.
On balance, the Government's record shows that its tight fiscal and monetary policies spurred on the recession, throwing people out of work and bankrupting small Canadian businesses, farmers and fishermen, among others. The irony of ironies is that the Government, driven by the Conservative obsession with reducing the deficit, actually contributed to its incredible borrowing requirement today. Instead of investing its deficit a few years ago, the Government tried to cut its spending at the same time as it tried to slow down the economy with high interest rates. We all know what that brought us: recession. The recession brought on by those policies actually increased the Government's borrowing requirements as close to two million Canadians were thrown out of work and on to welfare and Unemployment Insurance rolls.
When I spoke to the borrowing authority Bill a few months ago, I had a slim hope that the new budget would hold something different for Canadians than the dreadful mix of Conservative economic schemes with which we have lived for the past five or six years. It was a slim hope, but nevertheless I harboured it.
At that time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) seemed to be testing the waters to see how far he should go with economic stimulation in his new budget. However, when he brought down the budget on April 19, we did not receive the long-heralded economic stimulation and job creation. No, what we received was the promise of almost 1.5 million people unemployed for the rest of this year and not even a glimmer of hope of returning, by 1987, to the days of less than one million Canadians unemployed. What we received were grand statements about the Special Recovery Program which gives $2.4 billion to the private sector over the next four years, and additional spending on public capital projects of only $560 million this year, $760 million next year and only $390 million in the following year. That kind of spending will not go far at all in sponsoring economic recovery and job creation.
What we received with the April budget was another stab at identifying the private sector as the engine of economic recovery, another abdication of the Government's responsibility for directing economic development and planning in Canada, directing it to the likes of Canadian Pacific, Imperial Oil and the mines. I am not saying that the Government should take over and run the Canadian economy. However, what I am saying is that the Government has a responsibility to provide some long-term direction as to how the Canadian economy will develop for the benefit of Canadians, not for the benefit of the blue ribbon coupon clippers south of the border.
Therefore, by throwing $2.4 billion at big business over the next four years, the Government expects it will fuel investment and economic recovery. However, I would like to remind the Government that Canadian industry is now operating at only

I want to tell the House what a couple of spokespersons from the corporate world had to say about this situation, because it is probably the only kind of source some of my Tory friends to the right will consider seriously. Tom D'Aquino, President of the Business Council on National Issues, has said:
In the budget, Lalonde identified the private sector as the engine of economic growth ... but what if the private sector does not deliver because it can't, because the demand just isn't there.
Tom Van Zuiden, senior vice-president of finance for Dofasco, said:
Corporations are not going to expand just to get tax credits. They need expanded markets and the current economy is not such that further expansion in our industry is really warranted.
All this says to me is that the Government is heading in the wrong direction, that when it builds a recovery program around incentives for corporate investment at the same time as it is taking money out of the pockets of consumers, it is missing the boat. It is a shame for the Government to approach this House for authority to borrow an additional $14.7 billion when we can see that none of the economic programs the Government is sponsoring will turn the economy around or, in the long run, reduce Government borrowing requirements.
Finally, I want to make the point that the Government's economic policies are adrift. Rather than trying to do something positive about the recession, the Government gave Canadians lots of talk but not a lot of action on economic recovery. The April budget may have been good to big business, but it does not hold much hope for the rest of us looking forward to genuine economic recovery. The economic posture contained in the last budget is one of waiting and pinning our hopes on American recovery. It is exactly the kind of timid economic direction we have been told over and over again we could expect from a Progressive Conservative Government. I contend that Canadians deserve better.

Mr. Speaker, a few minutes ago the gallery of the House of Commons was filled with young people, people in their early' teens listening to the debate. I wondered as I watched them what legacy this Government will leave to these young people. Will it be a legacy of opportunity or will it be a legacy of bankruptcy, indebtedness and high taxes?
Really this is a sad debate. This Bill asks Parliament to approve the borrowing by this Government of some $14.7
billion. This is the seventh time in this session that the Government has come to Parliament for borrowing authority and has requested a total of some $81.5 billion.
Many people do not understand what a billion means. If you relate that $81.5 billion to millions, Mr. Speaker, that means $81,000 million. That is the amount of money this Government has asked permission to borrow in this session which started in 1980.
It is interesting to look back on the history of the Trudeau years and see what has happened to this great country of ours. It is a great country. It is a country rich in resources, natural, physical and human, and a country which has the greatest potential of any country in this world. But this Government has not developed that potential. It has done its best to stifle it. Personally, I suggest it is because of the philosophy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and this Government, a philosophy which embraces socialist and Marxist theories, believes in centralization and in government control. This "Big Daddy" syndrome has forced us into low productivity and has caused this country to end up with the highest unemployment record in history, high interest rates and an 80-cent dollar. The Government and the Prime Minsiter say: "Well, there is nothing we can do about it; this is a world-wide problem and basically the Americans are to blame. If the Americans can only pull out of their problems, then Canada will pull out as well."
It is interesting to examine what has happened in the last 15 or 20 years, that I call the Trudeau years. If one looks at the statistics, one will find that on a national accounts basis spending in 1968-69 was $12.6 billion. In 1983-84 it will be $100 billion, which in that period of time is an increase of some 693 per cent. If one looks at it on a public accounts basis, a basis commonly used, one will find that in 1968-69 expenditures were $12.3 billion. In 1983-1984 they will be $89.8 billion, or an increase of some 554 per cent.
Let me refer to the public debt. When the present Prime Minister took over as leader of this country, our gross public debt was $31 billion. At the end of 1981-82, the last figure that we are able to get, it was $134 billion. It is estimated that in 1982 the public debt will be about $165 billion. It is further estimated that by March 31, 1987 our net debt, that is after we take our assets away from our debts, will be some $232 billion.
What about the interest on this debt? Each and every taxpayer in this country is faced with the responsibility of paying the interest on this debt. In 1983-84 the interest on our national debt will be some $17.6 billion. That is about $700 for every man, woman and child in this country, or about $1,700 for every taxpayer. But let us look at the year 1968-69. The estimates, the total cost of running this country, in 1968-69 were about $12 billion. That $12 billion included all the cost of government, all the cost of defence; in fact, every expenditure
May 31, 1983

of government. Now we are asked to pay $17.5 billion just in interest alone. The burden is almost unbearable.
I always relate the Government to a farmer, a worker or a small business. If you spend more than you take in, you are in financial difficulties. That is what this Government has done and is doing. It is spending more than it is taking in, and it is borrowing far beyond its means to cover the portion it is not able to take in. The result is we are very close to being in a bankrupt position.
I have told groups of senior citizens that they are probably the most fortunate group who ever lived in Canada because at the present time they are in receipt of the old age pension, the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the Canada Pension Plan, a health care plan and New Horizons grants. But I have to say to them that it is unlikely their children, or your children or mine, Mr. Speaker, or their children's children, will enjoy those benefits because there will just not be the money to cover those types of programs. With increasing budgets, increasing national debt and the aging population there will be fewer and fewer taxpayers to pay the cost of those programs.
Let me ask once again: What legacy will we leave to our children and our children's children? Will we leave them a legacy of opportunity, or will we leave them a legacy of bankruptcy and indebtedness? Unless we change our ways, unless we curb our spending and unless we base our decisions on economics rather than politics, I am very much afraid the legacy we will leave to those children will be one of bankruptcy, indebtedness and high taxes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a veteran Member of this House recently told me of a colleague who had one standard speech format available for all occasions. No matter what the debate, the speech was appropriate with only minor modification made to suit the subject. All that was required was a five-minute preparation to fill in the blanks.
That type of style would be an extremely efficient format for Members of this House confronted with this Government's legislative finesse of the past few years, and particularly of the past few months. This Government under the guidance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and latterly under successive Finance Ministers, has increased Government expenditures from $12.3 billion to $89.8 billion in the past 15 years. The Government, through waste and irresponsible neglect of fundamental principles basic to even a child's understanding of economics, has left the nation's productive capacity in shambles, while blaming the catastrophe on all the world around us and never accepting responsibility or putting it where it belongs.
The combination of excessive spending and a shattered tax base from which to draw revenue has had the inevitable result of ever enlarging annual national deficits. Now the nation, which a few years ago was shocked at the prospect of an increase in the national debt of Canada $4 billion, hardly
Borrowing Authority
blinks an eye as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) declares a deficit in excess of $30 billion and notes that the national debt has doubled in the past five years and will double again in the next five years.
The nation hardly grasps the implication of the Minister of Finance's figures, which show that a third of the revenue of Canada, which comes mainly in the form of taxes that Canadians pay directly or indirectly to the treasury, goes simply to pay the interest on the national debt or that 20 per cent of the expenditures of Canada go for that unproductive purpose. One can only pause to wonder what figures will be presented to the House and the nation five years from now when the national debt has doubled from $120 billion to $240 billion, if the Minister and the Government are allowed to pursue their unrepentant ways.
This is a special concern considering a growing conviction which is occupying thoughtful Canadians and was contained in an article in today's edition of The Citizen of Ottawa, headlined "Large federal debt will force up interest rates". I will refer to this article later if time permits.
In this circumstance of spending excesses, the only certainty which exists is that the Government of Canada through its Finance Minister will be back repeatedly to lay claim to the right to appropriate more and more borrowed money to maintain its expensive, expansive ways.
Thus the original concept of a standard speech would be entirely appropriate to the House. On how many occasions could it have been used in the past few months? A standardized speech on borrowing authority legislation would have been useful on seven different occasions during this session of Parliament.
The obsession for spending which consumes the Government has been demonstrated in Bills C-30, C-59, C-111, C-125, C-128, C-143, and Bill C-151 which is presently being debated.
In fiscal year 1982-83 the Government came to the House four times to demand authority to borrow a total of $22.6 billion so that it could continue its habit of unrestrained extravagance. And where are we today? In its April budget the Government indicated that it would require $26.7 billion to make up the excess of its spending over its revenue during the current year. At present the Government has borrowing authority in place of some $16 billion. If the Minister of Finance is forecasting a shortfall of $26.7 billion and has a reserve of authority to borrow $16 billion, the demand we should be debating today should be for $10.7 billion.
Why, then, are we faced with a demand for nearly $15 billion ? I suggest it is because the Government does not have any faith in its own figures and, more specifically, it does not have any faith in its own discipline when it comes to curbing its appetite for spending. Government Members say: "Give us unlimited financing so that we can act as we have always acted-bestowing favour on our friends, using the largesse of the treasury for political advantage whenever and wherever it most pleases us and is seen to be to our advantage".

May 31, 1983
Borrowing Authority
We should contrast this attitude with that of the newly elected Government of British Columbia which campaigned on a platorm of restraint and realism. The people of British Columbia understood and appreciated this, as evidenced by the manifest rejection of the NDP call for actions of spending which are the duplicate of what the Government in Ottawa is presently inflicting upon Canada. Both the NDP and the Liberal Party opposite would be well advised to take note of the clear, decisive message which the electors of British Columbia provided. Canadians want their treasury to be treated rationally and reasonably-the type of restraint promised and being delivered by Premier Bennett of British Columbia.
1 would like to refer to an article which appeared in today's edition of The Globe and Mail headed "Curb needed in spending, Bennet says". It reads:
Without fiscal restraint, the British Columbia Government will accumulate deficits totally $12 billion in the next four years, Premier William Bennett said yesterday.
"Not only the provincial Government, but all provincial agencies and local Governments will be called on to exercise greater responsibility," Mr. Bennett told reporters .. .
"It is fair to say that every program of Government, every Government agency, every Crown corporation, every board, every commission-all are under complete review over the next few days and the next few weeks."
Mr. Bennett said the recession has ravaged Government revenue and he expects major shortfalls in tax income, particularly from corporations.
Where do we have any comparative degree of restraint shown by the Government of Canada? Of course, the answer is that we do not and will not have a comparative degree of restraint as long as this particular regime is in power.
Earlier I referred to an article in The Citizen by Seymour Friedland. It is in that context that I think we must be very concerned about what will happen five years from now when the national debt of Canada is double what it is presently because we have allowed the Government to continue in its unrepentant style of spending. An article entitled "Large federal debt will force up interest rates" quoted one Earl Bederman of the Canada Permanent Trust Company. 1 see Mr. Speaker is indicating that I have used up my allotted time, but the article reads:
Part of Bederman's pessimism is based on the recent Lalonde budget. Although it has received widespread acclaim, Bederman argues that it will have a depressing impact on the economy for the next four years.
I advise my colleagues opposite to read this particular article.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to speak for only ten minutes. This Bill is a symptom of the dreadfully serious mismanagement of the Canadian economy by its Government. Last year Canada ran dead last among the 24 member nations of the OECD. We placed 55th out of 81 countries in terms of economic performance, according to the publication "Euromoney". Some on this side feel that the Liberals have deliberately worsened the economy in order to fight inflation. We must ask ourselves, for example, how many of our constituents were put out of work because of the interest rate policy of the Government about a year ago?
As others have pointed out, this Bill will authorize the Government to borrow an additional $14.7 billion. It follows seven previous similar requests made by the Government in this Parliament. In his recent budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) indicated that the deficit for the coming year will be $31 billion, $28.8 billion for 1984-85, $26.7 billion for 1985-86 and $25.6 billion for 1986-87. That is $114 billion in the next four years. We must add to that the approximate $70 billion which those fiscal maniacs opposite ran up in borrowing in the eighties. That will be more than $200 billion before they are voted out of office in the next election.
Let me give some idea of their idea of irresponsible Government financing and what it is doing to this country. First, total Government spending in terms of the $100 billion the Government intends to spend next year is enough to buy a $100,000 home for every household in Alberta.
Second, the cost of interest on the debt exceeds the value of all federal income taxes collected from persons earning less than $50,000 a year.
Third, the Government's gross debt is the equivalent of $6,400 per capita and $16,000 per taxpayer. That is outrageous.
Fourth, in private industry, an enterprise with revenue that was only 70 per cent of its expenditures and gross debt that was four times the net value of its assets would be forced into bankruptcy. Where is there a place for those opposite to file for bankruptcy on behalf of their fellow citizens?
Fifth, the Liberals will spend between 1980-81 and 1983-84 a total of $49 billion more than had been planned in the Conservative budget when we were in office. That is $4,900 per taxpayer.
Sixth, the federal Government spends money at the rate of $274 million per day, $11 million per hour and $190,000 per minute. At that rate, $19 million was spent during the budget speech of the Minister of Finance.
Seventh, including operating deficits and capital expenditures, Mirabel airport today, as an example of the profligacy on the other side, has cost the taxpayers more than $700 million. That sum of money is the equivalent of giving 800,000 Canadians a free round-trip ticket from St. John's, Newfoundland to Vancouver, British Columbia.
May 31, 1983

Eighth, the federal Government has an information and advertising budget of $245 million a year, the largest of its kind in Canada. That sum of money is 18 times the total cost of Government in the first year of Confederation.
Ninth, in 1981 the federal Government spent $13.1 million on food, liquor and entertainment. I wonder how much of that was spent on other than Liberal friends. That is the equivalent of more than one million bottles of liquor.
Finally, the deficit this year will be $31.3 billion. If that incredible amount of money were turned into $1 bills and laid end to end, it would stretch just under three million miles. That is the equivalent of travelling the Trans-Canada Highway and back 304 times. The line would stretch to the moon and back six times.
What else can we say but that the Government is grossly irresponsible? It is doing its best to bankrupt the country, aided and abetted by its annex in the New Democratic Party. 1 sometimes wonder which is the annex of which. I ask that in light of the Gallup poll which came out a week ago. It indicated that 30 per cent of Liberal supporters favour a greater role for the private sector, contrasted to 41 per cent for NDP supporters, the Party of the Regina Manifesto, and 61 per cent for supporters of this Party.
The point is that the supporters of the new Democratic Party are now more in favour of private enterprise than the supporters of the Government Party. Times are changing and I cannot explain it. Maybe the New Democratic Party or the Liberals can explain it. Somebody looking at this country from Mars would consider that we were being run by a group of lunatics.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise and speak again on this borrowing authority Bill which is in the order of $14.7 billion, of which something in the order of $4 billion is completely unaccounted for. Speculation runs high that that $4 billion would make a fairly substantial contribution to an election slush fund, paid out at something of the order of $10 million a day. That is a very serious matter. The matter of this House authorizing legislation to borrow taxpayers' money should receive a very careful and scrupulous accounting. If the Government is going to borrow that money, it should be targeted to specific projects that will fulfil a community need, an employment need and a need for economic development at
Borrowing Authority
this time. We do not see that occurring with the present initiatives of the Liberal Government.
Today I call to the attention of the House and the Minister some areas where it could allocate the $4 billion instead of dropping in into a slush fund. It is opportune that we have with us in the Chamber at this time the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). I recall to the Minister of Transport the need for an airport in the community of Bella Bella, B.C. Over the years that community of approximately 1,000 people has been looking for Government support by way of a borrowing authority Bill or a contribution. This is an excellent project and is worth studying. It is a native community with very high unemployment. There is a hospital in that community from which they evacuate people with difficult medical problems. There is an RCMP law enforcement establishment in the community and there are schools in the community.
It desperately needs an airport. The people have virtually scratched out of the ground by their own means the beginnings of an airport and, for a very nominal sum of money, could extend the airport runway to 3,500 feet which would accommodate not only their community but other communities on the central coast. Instead of spending that money, Mr. Speaker, It would appear that the Minister of Transport and his officials have decided that they would rather support an airport on another island.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1983-84 (NO. 2) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
It would be very nice if the Minister would not pass the buck on to the Government of British Columbia but fulfil his Government's federal responsibility to native people through the mechanism of the borrowing Act by allocating assistance to the Indian community of Bella Bella.
There is no justification for allowing any government to go ahead and move a facility which is so desperately needed to an island with only 60 residents. I hope that my old friend, the Minister of Transport, will find in his heart a willingness to come forward and support that community of Bella Bella and the development on the central coast that will stem from it. I believe this is vitally important, Mr. Speaker. This is an important use for the funds that have not been accounted for in the borrowing authority.
The borrowing authority is an important mechanism by which funds can be allocated. It is interesting to note that the Ministers often complain that they do not have any money. Well, here in the borrowing authority it looks as if $4 billion has not yet been accounted for or allocated. The Government would like to see the House ratify the borrowing authority.
I bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport another project that is needed in the community of Bella Bella and which illustrates what I am trying to point out. If the Minister of Transport or the Government of Canada are looking for some way to account for those funds, the community of Bella Bella desperately needs a roll-on/roll-off ferry facility. The

May 31, 1983
Borrowing Authority
cost of living in that community is so astronomically high that it cripples any economic development that would benefit the approximately 1,000 people who live there. The cost of food is prohibitively high. Elere in Ottawa we live in luxury in terms of the cost of food and facilities. The situation in Bella Bella could be changed, however, if the Government were to provide support for a roll-on/roll-off ferry facility. It is a nominal cost to create such enormous benefits in that community.
I hope that when the Government makes an evaluation about what it wants to do with that $4 billion it is asking the House to vote for, the Minister of Transport will provide that ferry facility for that Bella Bella. It would be very useful if the Minister of Transport could look at that project very carefully and find it within himself to support it as one of the priorities of the $4 billion.
In looking for ways to spend that $4 billion fund that has not yet been allocated, another very interesting application of those funds might be found in the community of Powell River. The community of Powell River has a single major industry, and its example is duplicated in many areas across the country. There are problems created by single industry communities. For instance, the pulp and paper mill in the community of Powell River has cut back production and has laid off 500 people. In a small community such as this, the lay-off of 500 people has a devastating effect. The people cannot move out because the housing market is depressed. There is no other source of employment in that community and the pulp mill will be virtually unable to rehire many of those people. The federal Government could provide support for work-sharing programs in that community. Even the apprentices who were laid off could be rehired to allow them to finish their training. The $4 billion that has not yet been allocated could be used in Powell River.
In addition, certain kinds of economic development could go ahead in a community such as Powell River, but initial support is needed. That initial support could help to diversify and strengthen the economy of a single industry community so that the boom and bust phenomenon would no longer occur. But that support is not forthcoming. It would be my hope that the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) and other influential members of the Government would look at Powell River when addressing the question of how to spend the extra $4 billion. I hope they would look seriously at creating employment opportunities, at creating job sharing opportunities as a short-term arrangement, and then look finally at assisting a single industry community such as Powell River to create some kind of diversity in its local economy so that it can take the boom and bust phenomenon out of the economy and allow people to have some kind of employment security.
While I am on the subject and the Ministers are present and listening, I would like to call three communities in the Comox Valley to their attention. These are the communities of Courtenay, Cumberland and Comox. The community of Comox has an air base which is proposing to move approximately 500 people to another area of the country to reduce the size of that
facility. Those 500 people, their families and their children will be removed from the valley. This will in fact have a very dramatic impact on the economy of that community. The community has already been hard hit by a recession and by the slowdown in the forest industries, and this is the present that they are to receive from the federal Government. I recognize why this is in fact being done, but certainly when 500 pay cheques are removed from a community with a stroke of a pen, the economy of that community is harmed.
Certain things can be done with this $4 billion slush fund that seems to be unaccounted for that would assist the communities in the Comox Valley. The Government could attempt to help the community with some offsets, and there are a number of offsets available. Hopefully, the Government would be concerned enough to provide the community with an alternate, such as another branch of the Canadian Armed Forces that could use the facility that is already there. The facilities are ideal for Sea King helicopter training. There are many other projects for which the federal Government could provide the offsets and opportunities after having caused a great deal of harm by removing 500 pay cheques from Comox.
It would be my hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Government would be in a position, through the $4 billion that is unaccounted for to begin to address some of these very serious problems that are faced by these people.

Mr. Speaker, I represent 87,980 people who live in North Vancouver-Burnaby. Each one of those households operates on a budget. They have so much coming in as income and they have so much going out for rent, food and other expenses. If expenses exceed income, the first thing that the householders would do is to look for a way to cut back and change that situation. This may mean, of course, that there will be spaghetti for dinner instead of hamburger. That is logical, but the Government is incapable of such plain common sense.
Anyone who operates a business works on the basis of a yearly cash flow statement which will indicate to him what he is taking in and what his expenses are. Hopefully there may be a little profit left over. If there is no profit and the businessman sees that he is going into the hole, then obviously he must cut expenditures or increase revenue. Again, this is just plain common sense. But the Government seems to be totally incompetent and totally incapable of understanding such plain common sense.
It might be interesting for my constituents to know that all 87,980 of them are in debt to the extent of $1,600 and that every taxpayer in the riding is in debt to the tune of $16,000 as a result of the Liberal Government. I am reminded of the story of one of my constituents who just had a baby. He immediately rushed to Lion's Gate Hospital, looked through the nursery window at his child and said: "Congratulations, my child, you are now $1,600 in debt. A few years from now when you become a taxpayer, you will automatically be $16,000 in debt, unless we can elect a Conservative Government and turn this kind of loose spending around."
May 31, 1983

How does the Government do it, Mr. Speaker? What is a supplementary estimate? It is an admission of failure. Seven times the Government has come back to Parliament for supplementary estimates in this Session of Parliament. That is seven admissions of failure-seven admissions that it cannot figure out what it is doing with the money.
We could talk about the $12 billion or $14 billion which was granted before, but let us look at the last 11 months. If this does not demonstrate incompetence on the part of the Government, 1 do not know what does. Eleven months ago the Government got $6.6 billion; nine months ago $11 billion; six months ago $4 billion; two months ago $19 billion; and today $14.7 billion. It has received $77.3 billion over a three-year period, or about $25 billion per year.
It might interest my constituents to know that they have a Liberal Government which is borrowing at the rate of $2 billion per month and that it has been doing this for years, to the detriment of the country. It is a Government gone mad. I would point out to my constituents that every dollar the Government borrows means one less dollar available for them to borrow for any purpose. This has an effect on interest rates and on the confidence the world has in Canada. When the Government is a mad spender you cannot expect investors to have much faith in it. As a result, in the last year alone $10 billion has left Canada. We will never know how many jobs that would have provided for Canadians had it remained in this country. We know why the money left Canada, however- because of the borrowing of $2 billion per month, month in and month out, that the Liberal regime has foisted on the public.
The foregoing is not all of the borrowing, Mr. Speaker; it is only the things that we know about. How many debts do Crown corporations have that are disguised as loans? How many debts do Crown corporations have disguised as letters of credit? How much are they showing as assets on the books, such as buggy whips, which should be written off and accepted as a loss? The Opposition cannot get that information from the Government and I can understand why it must be kept a deep, dark secret. It must be a source of continual embarrassment that such terrible things are even suspected.
A succession of Auditors General have told us that spending is out of control. You do not have to be very bright to know that, Mr. Speaker. The Government has the authority to spend but it has no responsibility.
When I first came to this House I served on the Public Accounts Committee-until I gave up in disgust. 1 remember asking an official of the Treasury Board what I thought was a very key question. I wanted to know what happens when a bureaucrat makes a colossal error, such as the overspending on the Calgary Airport, or architects designing buildings that drop into the muskeg, or any of the other scandals that have happened with this Government. 1 wanted to know the penalty for someone who did not know what he was doing in his job- the penalty for a Government official who wastes money. The answer I got from Treasury Board was that there are no penalties. As my colleague says, the chances are that the
Borrowing Authority
official would be promoted because it would be an embarrassment to leave him in the same position. But no bureaucrat is afraid of his job or is prepared to take the responsibility as well as the authority when he spends money.
I could go on with a thousand stories and it would take all day, Mr. Speaker, but I have two or three that 1 would draw to your attention. This year the CBC wants $820 million. 1 wonder if the Canadian people are prepared to spend $820 million over and above the revenue of the CBC. As well, $45 million is required for the Official Languages Act and the metric Commission wants $32 million. The Metric Commission is a good example of what I call the rise of bureaucrats. In 1974 its total budget was $44,000 but it has managed to get that up to $32 million. Today, its payroll is $3.2 million. The Consolidated Computer caper wasted $125 million. Some of the bureaucrats responsible for that should have been hanged by their thumbs.
I would like to see one budget, totally complete and fully explained in simple terms but no supplementary supply and no borrowing. If the managers cannot do that they should be given their running shoes. If the Cabinet cannot do it, that should be the greatest news story in Canada.
There are 12 American States where the people, through the native shrewdness that enables them to survive, have passed laws requiring that the budget of the State must be balanced. We may see that sort of thing here. This country will not have fiscal responsibility until this crew of drunken sailors and spendthrifts is thrown out of office, the sooner the better. 1 do not mean Government restraint on the backs of the poor. What I mean is financial responsibility on the heads of the wasteful bureaucrats who spend, spend, spend, without a thought for you and me, the overburdened taxpayer.
Mir. Mel Gass (Malpeque): Mr. Speaker, we are once again witnessing the federal Government's need for parliamentary authority to borrow new money. Prior to this Winter, the Government had never had to use its emergency borrowing powers. To date the Government has come to Parliament seven times in this session to ask Parliament for more borrowing authority. We need only to recall Bills C-30, C-59, C-111, C-125, C-128, C-143 and now C-151. In fiscal 1982-83 alone, the Government came to Parliament four times to seek borrowing authority.
The Government has borrowing authority of $16 billion in the 1983-84 fiscal year. Bil C-143 had provided for up to $2 billion of the $5 billion of authority it granted for fiscal 198283 to be carried over into fiscal 1983-84 if it was not used. Bill C-143 also provided for $14 billion to be granted for this year, fiscal 1983-84.
Based on its financial requirements of $26.7 billion and existing borrowing authority of $16 billion, the Government needs $10.7 billion in additional authority this year. Bill C-151 provided for $14.7 billion in new authority-$4 billion more than is indicated by the financial requirements. Of this, $2 billion does not have to be used this year and may be carried

May 31, 1983
Borrowing Authority
forward into the future. The Government thus has a cushion of $2 billion for this year, plus a cushion of $2 billion to be used in any year. The money that is carried over in this bill does not have to be used next year and could be carried over indefinitely. The Government already has $16 billion in borrowing authority for this year, more than enough to last until summer. The past history of the federal Government is proof positive that it has mismanaged our country's finances and now must borrow more money to make ends meet.
Let us examine the federal Government's spending and the deficit which will outline the Government's mismanagement of the country's economy. Over the past 15 years, Government spending has risen at an unprecedented rate. On a national accounts basis spending has climbed from $12.6 billion in 1968-69 to an estimated $100.2 billion in 1983-84, an increase of 693 per cent. Spending has increased from $12.3 billion in 1968-69 to $89.8 billion, an increase of 554 per cent. Relative to fiscal 1979-80, spending has risen by 78 per cent on a public accounts basis or 84 per cent on a national accounts basis. In 1983-84, the Government plans to spend $20 billion more on a national accounts basis than the Progressive Conservative Government had planned to spend, and will borrow $22 billion more than the Progressive Conservatives had planned to borrow.
For every $3 the Government spends, it must borrow $1. A deficit can be financed only by printing money or by borrowing. In 1982, borrowing by the federal Government accounted for 51 per cent of all net new security issues placed in Canada. Borrowing of that magnitude clearly must have an effect on the supply and demand for money, and thus on the interest rates which must be borne by the private sector. The budget points to a deficit in excess of $25 billion for each of the next four years.
At the end of the 1981-82 fiscal year, the gross debt was $134 billion. The gross debt was probably between $160 billion and $165 billion as of March 31, 1983. In comparison, the gross debt was $31 billion when the present Government took office. The net debt was $120.1 billion as of March 31, 1983. This compares to $16.2 billion in March, 1968. Since the Government resumed power in 1980, the net debt has almost doubled from its March 31, 1980 level of $68.6 billion. In the coming year, one public accounts revenue dollar in three, or one expenditure dollar in five, will be used to pay interest on the debt.
There is the ever-growing interest burden. Interest on the debt cost an estimated $17.6 billion, the equivalent of $700 for every man, woman and child in Canada, or $1,700 per taxpayer, just for interest. Interest on the debt in 1983-84 will equal 4.6 per cent of Canada's Gross National Product. This compares to 2 per cent when Trudeau first took office.

I apologize, Mr. Speaker. The third cost is that productive private sector borrowing is crowded out and interest rates rise. In the 1982 calendar year, federal Government borrowing accounted for 51 per cent of the net new security issues placed in Canada. If there was less federal Government borrowing, there would be less demand for money and interest rates would be lower. At the time of the 1980 election, the Bank of Canada rate was 14 per cent, the average mortgage rate was 13.5 per cent, and the chartered bank prime rate was 15 per cent. By August, 1981 the bank rate had climbed to a record 21.24 per cent, chartered bank prime was 22.75 per cent, and some lenders were charging in excess of 22 per cent for first mortgages.
While interest rates have fallen significantly over the past few months, the reason for this stems from factors other than sound economic management. First, the recession has created a shortage of demand for new loans and a significant increase in the level of deposits. The savings rate is at record heights. People are afraid to spend money out of fear for the future, and they are justified because of the actions of this Government. The forces of supply and demand are thus partly responsible for the decline in rates. Economic recovery will mean the end of this source of downward pressure.
Second, there has been a sharp decline in interest rates in the United States. Any increase in U.S. interest rates will send Canadian interest rates back up again.
Third, because the current economic recession has hit Canada more severely than any of our major trading partners, our demand for imported goods has fallen sharply while our exports have remained relatively stable. This has taken some of the pressure off the dollar, which has been propped up by high interest rates. Economic recovery will end this temporary phenomenon.
The Government will argue that lower inflation is responsible for the drop in interest rates. In fact, the factors outlined above have had a far greater role. Indeed, a significant part of the decline in the inflation rate is due to the recession, which is hardly a sign of sound economic management. This year the financial requirements of the Government will be equal to 84 per cent of expected personal savings.
The fourth cost is that of confidence and it is possibly our greatest. The investment community does not trust a Government which continues to live so far beyond its means. They do not want to hold a currency which continues to be debased by excessive Government borrowing. As a consequence, the dollar has fallen, thus driving up the cost of living in Canada. Interest rates remain high as the Government attempts to support the dollar. Job creating capital investment has gone elsewhere. The financial requirements of the Government of Canada over the next four years will total $93.2 billion. Bills C-143 and C-151 are just the tip of the iceberg.
The Government's credit is certainly damaged when it comes to the unemployment issue. The national unemployment rate in February was 12.5 per cent, which means 1,585,000 Canadians were out of work. Four hundred and nine thousand Canadians worked part-time because they could not find full-
May 31, 1983

time employment. These unemployment totals do not include 149,000 discouraged people who have given up looking for work because there are no jobs available. In February, the youth unemployment rate was 20.7 per cent and in August, 1982 183,000 fewer students had a summer job than was the case in August, 1981. How can Parliament possibly support additional funding for a Government which has two million out of work and close to that number are on welfare? Unemployment Insurance benefits are running out and the Government does not offer concrete proposals which deal with this serious situation. In 1982 Unemployment Insurance payments totalled $8.6 billion. It is this very high unemployment rate which has been contributing to the increase in estimated financial requirements since October, 1982. By permitting the Government of Canada to borrow an additional $19 billion to finance the escalating spending deficit, now over $26 billion, Parliament is increasing the national debt to $160 billion.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that my time is almost up. I have one last comment and that is that I believe very firmly in the adage that somewhere, sometime, somebody has to pay. I also believe that the "sometime" is getting very close and the "somebody" is our young people.
Mir. Howard Crosby (Halifax West): Mr. Speaker, this is the seventh time in the current session that the Government has presented to Parliament a Bill to authorize the borrowing of a vast amount of money. This has been pointed out by other Hon. Members but I would like to underline that fact. Bill C-151, which enacts yet another borrowing authority, makes provision for the raising of an additional $14.7 billion.
On several occasions, Mr. Speaker, I have underlined the practical effect on Canadians of the enormous federal Government borrowings. Let me stress the fact that today most of the funds borrowed by the Government are used to meet current account spending deficits and not to construct public works and undertakings of an enduring nature. Annual borrowing to meet current spending deficits has a two-fold effect on Canadians, especially Canadian taxpayers. First, it increases dramatically the debt load which must be borne by all Canadians in the form of increased contributions to Government revenues. Second, the Government competes directly with Canadian businesses and individuals for available investment funds.
In the result, rates of interest on all forms of loans, from consumer car loans to loans for industrial expansion, are escalated upward. At present the interest rate is low, not because of Government policy but because industrial activity and consumer spending are at an all-time low. As we search for economic recovery, we need assurance that increased activity will not increase interest rates to the dramatic levels experienced in 1982 or we will be faced with a new burst of double-digit inflation.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, expressing the effect of the federal Government borrowing in simple factual terms, we are now utilizing over 25 per cent of annual revenues to pay interest charges. In addition, we are burdening 11 million Canadian taxpayers with an individual debt share of over
Borrowing Authority
$2,500 this current year, with a total debt share of over $20,000. To this burden must be added any provincial Government debt the taxpayer shares as residents of a particular Province. All of these Government debts must be repaid by Canadian taxpayers, or passed on to future generations. That is a poor legacy to pass on to our children and grandchildren.
When we consider the current state of the Government's purse, we realize and recognize the certain need for restraint in public spending. But we need real reductions in expenditure, not programs like the Government's six and five restraint which stresses perception and not fact. The Government pretends to save by cutting payments to senior citizens, young persons and retired public servants and then squanders money on Crown corporations like the post office, Canadian National Railways and projects like Mirabel airport and the Gulfspan ferry. To quote an example which is currently in the news in Nova Scotia, there is the $62 million loss on the investment in the CAST shipping group. Every time I stand in this House I remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that was money thrown away. He was warned in advance, yet he allowed it to happen.
With spending restraint in mind, Mr. Speaker, let me consider some special areas of concern in Nova Scotia, indeed throughout Atlantic Canada, which are relevant to the financial status of the Government. We all know restraint must be exercised but we also should know that it must be implemented in a careful and prudent manner and in the hope and expectation that the Canadian economy can be restored to prosperity in the years ahead. Contemplating the fact that we will have a new Government and new direction in policy, I think we can look ahead seriously to the day when the Canadian economy will be restored to its former prosperity.
Let me examine some of those special interest areas such as the educational system. The Government with its alleged restraint has cut back on payments to universities and other post-secondary institutions to the extent of over $1 billion. This comes at a time when we need to provide education and train Canadians. Yet the Government, by keeping back this sum of money from our young people seeking an education, puts an additional burden on those 500,000 university students because it will become necessary in this and ensuing academic years to increase tuition fees.
Canadians are proud that we have an educational system which offers the opportunity to young Canadians to seek university level education if they have the academic ability to perform. But now we are placing that in jeopardy. That is a negative step in two ways. First, it destroys the initiative of young Canadians who do not now see an opportunity for advanced education. Second, it fails to provide Canada with the qualified work force we need to take advantage of the move to a technological economy. That is the kind of reduction in spending which has no productive effect. In fact, it is very damaging and we will realize this in future years.
The April budget spoke of a Special Recovery Program and allocated over $4 billion to the program. Some of it was to be

May 31. 1983
Borrowing Authority
for special projects, over 100 of which were to take place across Canada. One of the most important projects from the point of view of Atlantic Canada was the allocation for marine transportation, specifically vessel procurement. Some $630 million was alleged to be allocated in the April budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). But when we come to examine that in greater detail we find that a great portion of that money was to construct vessels for the Canadian Coast Guard and it was merely an acceleration of an existing program.
The net increase in expenditure is much less than the $300 million first indicated. We on the East Coast are very concerned about the plight of our shipyards, indeed all shipyards across Canada. We realize there must be an acceleration of Government vessel construction programs, both in the Coast Guard and the Department of Transport, more particularly in the Department of National Defence. The patrol frigate program, which is a $1 billion program to provide six modern vessels to the Canadian navy, must be accelerated but no mention was made of that in the budget. So we wonder how serious the Government is when it talks about accelerating activity in the shipbuilding industry.
In budgetary terms, in national defence we have undertaken to honour our commitment to NATO to expand and re-equip the Canadian Armed Forces. The budget lost sight of this and again we have this unproductive restraint. By investing in equipment to the Canadian Armed Forces we not only create jobs and activity for Canadians, but we also create an enduring asset for the future, one which will, in effect, save money by acting now. So 1 urge the Government to take a look at defence expenditures and make sure that some action is taken to improve equipment in the Armed Forces, particularly to upgrade the Canadian Navy through the patrol frigate program.
I want to speak of a local matter which is of great concern, the recent announcement that the contract for the refit of the HMCS Nipigon will go to Davie Shipbuilding in Lauzon, Quebec. This multimillion dollar contract would have made a great difference to the work force at the Halifax shipyards. With the loss of this contract we can expect an empty shipyard, for which the Liberal Member from Halifax will have to answer. He knows the difficulties which have occurred there.
1 want to speak briefly of the fishing industry because in restraining Government expenditures the Government has apparently forgotten about its obligation to the Atlantic fishing industry. The task force report would require an expenditure of $300 million over and above the improvement of facilities at small craft harbours, but there is no provision for this.
We have to have some control over the offshore oil industry.
I read in the paper that Husky-Bow Valley are going to expand activity in their project, yet they are going to use a drill
rig imported from Norway. How does that create jobs for Canadians?
Let me end on this note, Mr. Speaker. While we appreciate and recognize that there must be restraints in Government expenditure, and while we oppose increases in borrowing, we want the Government to be responsible in its administration of the programs we now have on our books.

subtopic: JURISDICTION OVER ARCTIC OCEAN SEABED
JURISDICTION OVER ARCTIC OCEAN SEABED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is high time that the Government of Canada made a firm
May 31, 1983

statement on the extent of its claim to sovereignty over the seabed of the Arctic Ocean.
Do we claim to exercise exclusive jurisdiction over the seabed within the entire sector extending from Canada's east-west extremities to the North Pole, or is the Government satisfied with something less?
At the time of the debate on the Canada Oil and Gas Act the Government was deliberately vague on the question. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the second annual meeting of federal, provincial, and territorial Ministers responsible for the Status of Women opened this morning with great expectations. I congratulate the federal Minister for hosting this important conference. We sincerely hope that positive action will result from this year's deliberations.
The situation for women has worsened considerably in one year. Future employment prospects are dismal. Lip service is not enough. All Governments must back up their intentions by committing the necessary resources.
This morning the federal Government unfortunately could not report the implementing of mandatory affirmative action which should be an example for Provinces to follow. Provinces called for a greater federal commitment to educational upgrading and training, particularly for high tech jobs and non-traditional jobs in the future. Adequate pay and protection for women working part-time, and extension of affordable child care, are other issues which urgently require joint action.
While Provinces have gained greater awareness of inequities, most have a long way to go in establishing strong, independent Ministries responsible for the Status of Women. 1 regret that British Columbia did not send either a Minister or a Deputy Minister to this very important meeting. Several Provinces, notably Quebec, Newfoundland, and Manitoba, reported positive programs which are models for other Provinces to follow. However, as the Minister from Quebec stated, it is a long march toward autonomy and equality for women. The march, at least, has begun.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING-CALL FOR CUT IN SPENDING PLANS
GOVERNMENT BORROWING-CALL FOR CUT IN SPENDING PLANS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the increase in interest rates, signalled last week by our Bank of Canada rate going to 9.5 per cent, the second substantial increase in two weeks, indicates that the demand by Government to Finance deficits is already starting to crowd out the demand by business for funds, and is already starting to push up interest rates.
The Government must act immediately to change its fiscal plan, to cut back on its borrowing requirements, and to give strong signals to the marketplace that it will not be borrowing moneys indicated in the budget and that it will be reassessing its deficit and spending plans. If there is no immediate change in the Government's borrowing stance, then it is very likely that interest rates will rise rapidly and that any hopes for a recovery will be squashed.
Before the interest rate increase trend sets in too firmly, the Government must act dramatically. The Government could easily cut its spending plans by 5 per cent. This would reduce its borrowing by $5 billion and would significantly reduce the anticipated pressures on financial markets. Moreover, it would indicate to markets that the Government is prepared to be responsible with respect to its debt management. We cannot afford another round of high interest rates.
